article: Where should you look for the ingredients that give a supplement gummy its texture?
Read the U.S. Supplement Facts panel and the ingredient list as separate parts of one label.
U.S. FDA dietary supplement labeling guidance on dietary ingredients and other ingredients.
copy: A Supplement Facts panel lists declared dietary ingredients and their amounts. A separate ingredient statement can identify other things in the product, such as what makes a gummy hold together or how a capsule is made. Reading only the panel can leave out relevant formulation details.
Read below the main panel as well

If you are comparing products with the same listed vitamin amount, check the other ingredients on each one. A dietary ingredient amount does not tell you what provided the texture, flavor or coating. Likewise, the presence of an ingredient on the label does not establish a clinical effect.
Use the complete current package if an ingredient matters to your decision. Two flavors from the same seller can have different ingredient lists.

article: Does a 90-capsule supplement bottle always provide 90 servings?
Calculate two package examples using the actual number of capsules per listed serving.
FDA net quantity and Supplement Facts guidance. Package arithmetic is hypothetical.
copy: A package count states how many capsules are inside. The Supplement Facts serving size says how many capsules make one listed serving. A 90-capsule bottle with two capsules per serving has 45 full servings. A bottle with three per serving has 30.
Count complete listed servings

Days of supply are another calculation because directions and actual use can differ from a count of servings. A cost comparison based on capsule count can mislead if each package uses a different serving. Use the size stated for the ingredient amount instead of assuming one capsule gives the whole number.
For your own comparison, write the price per labeled serving next to the package count. This lets you compare matching units.

article: Why can a children’s supplement show two Daily Value percentages for the same amount?
Read the population headings before comparing two percentages on a U.S. label.
FDA U.S. updated Nutrition and Supplement Facts guidance and example labels.
copy: A label can use different Daily Value references for different groups. If a product shows more than one column, the same ingredient amount may correspond to different percentages. The table heading identifies who the percentage is for.
Follow each percentage up to its heading

For a product comparison, copy the amount and its units before copying the percentages. A percentage can change because the reference changed, even when the amount stayed the same. Also check the labeled serving because a product might use separate servings for different age groups.
A label reference is a comparison tool. It does not set an individual child’s needs or tell a caregiver which product is suitable.

article: Why isn’t 1,250 mg calcium carbonate the same as 1,250 mg calcium?
Use the NIH calcium fact sheet to distinguish compound weight from elemental calcium on a label.
NIH ODS calcium fact sheet and FDA labeling guidance. Hypothetical compound masses used to explain the units.
copy: Calcium carbonate is about 40% calcium by weight, so 1,250 mg of that compound corresponds to about 500 mg calcium. The elemental amount is the figure you compare across calcium products. Calcium citrate contains a smaller proportion of calcium by weight.
Compare the line that says calcium

On U.S. Supplement Facts, the stated amount for calcium describes the declared calcium, with the form often listed beside it. If the row already says 500 mg calcium, do not apply the 40% calculation again to that figure. A description of the raw compound uses a different basis.
Keep the form and the elemental amount together in your notes. A label comparison does not set a personal supplement regimen.

article: What does 325 mg ferrous sulfate mean next to 65 mg iron?
Separate the labeled salt weight from the measured amount of iron in a verified U.S. drug-label example.
U.S. DailyMed ferrous sulfate labels and NIH ODS iron fact sheet. Amounts illustrate label interpretation, not an intake recommendation.
copy: A ferrous sulfate product can list 325 mg of the compound and state that this provides 65 mg iron. In that label example, the two numbers describe the same unit, not two amounts of iron to add together. For comparisons with another form, use the declared elemental iron.
Keep the two fields distinct

Check the exact product. Different salts and formulations can use different compound weights for similar elemental amounts. Do not infer the elemental amount from the word sulfate alone when a verified product label is available.
Read the per-unit or per-serving information and follow the actual product directions. This comparison explains the numbers, without recommending how much iron to take.

article: Why can the same probiotic be labeled Lactobacillus on one package and Lacticaseibacillus on another?
Use the original classification paper and a label to check the species and strain code.
Original 2020 bacterial taxonomy revision and manufacturer example. A name match alone does not establish efficacy.
copy: A taxonomy revision changed the genus names for many organisms that were previously called Lactobacillus. An older article can use Lactobacillus rhamnosus and a newer label can use Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus. You still need to check the strain identifier when linking a product with a study.
Compare the strain code alongside the name

For the well-known GG example, look for the same species and GG strain designation in context. The taxonomy change does not make all strains with that species name interchangeable. It also does not establish the product’s quantity, storage condition or evidence for an advertised outcome.
Record the name as printed and the relevant synonym when cataloging products. That makes later searches easier without merging distinct strains.

article: Does shelf-stable mean two probiotics have the same count by expiry?
Compare storage conditions with a separate viable-count statement on a supplement label.
Culturelle manufacturer product information and NIH ODS probiotic fact sheet. Storage details are version-specific.
copy: Shelf-stable describes storage under the stated conditions. It does not tell you how another probiotic’s viable count compares at the end of its shelf life. A product can list a quantity in colony-forming units and give separate instructions about temperature and moisture.
Read both statements for the actual package

Look for whether the count is guaranteed through the date shown and which storage conditions apply. Use the listed serving size if you compare counts. Product formulations and packaging can differ, so refrigeration status alone is a poor basis for choosing a higher count.
A count describes viable organisms under conditions. Match the strain and studied outcome separately when assessing a health claim.

article: How do you translate a calcium supplement’s Daily Value percentage into milligrams?
Work through a U.S. reference-label example and see why to prefer the printed amount.
NIH and FDA U.S. adult and age-four-plus labeling reference of 1,300 mg. Example percentages are illustrative.
copy: For a U.S. label that uses a 1,300 mg calcium Daily Value, 20% corresponds to about 260 mg by arithmetic. The label’s declared milligrams give the more direct comparison. A displayed percentage can be rounded and may use a different reference for a different intended group.
Use the printed amount first

If both products use the same reference and serving basis, a displayed 50% corresponds to about 650 mg. Keep that relationship attached to calcium. The same percentage for a different nutrient uses another denominator. You also need to account for how many tablets make one listed serving.
Use this calculation to read the label, without treating the label reference as an intake recommendation.

article: Why can two older vitamin E labels with the same IU list different milligrams?
Use NIH conversions to compare the natural and synthetic vitamin E forms on older labels.
NIH ODS U.S. vitamin E unit conversions for natural and synthetic alpha-tocopherol forms.
copy: An older label that uses international units needs a form-specific conversion. NIH gives about 0.67 mg per IU for natural alpha-tocopherol and 0.45 mg per IU for synthetic alpha-tocopherol. Two labels showing 100 IU can therefore describe about 67 mg and 45 mg respectively.
Identify the form before converting the units

The form is often shown as d-alpha or dl-alpha on older labels. Read the complete name and whether the amount already appears in milligrams. If it does, a second conversion would change the amount incorrectly. If the form is unavailable, the historical IU figure is not enough for an exact comparison.
The arithmetic helps translate units. It does not establish the relative clinical effects of finished products.

article: Does a label saying vitamin K2 identify the exact form used in a trial?
Use the NIH vitamin K terminology to identify the reported menaquinone before comparing products.
NIH ODS information on phylloquinone and menaquinone forms. No medication or intake guidance.
copy: Vitamin K2 refers to a family of compounds called menaquinones. A product labeled K2 may name MK-4 or MK-7, among other possibilities. The broader term does not identify a single trial intervention or say which form a researcher measured.
Read the form as part of the ingredient name

Match the compound, units and serving before comparing a label with a paper. Also check whether the outcome was a blood measurement, a marker or something experienced by participants. A higher listed microgram amount does not make different forms interchangeable for that purpose.
Keep a missing subtype unresolved rather than guessing from the term K2. This guide describes label identity and does not address changes to medication or supplementation.

article: Why is a creatinine result different from directly measured filtration in a creatine trial?
Read a primary trial by the method used to assess kidney filtration.
Original study of creatine and filtration measurements in resistance-trained adults consuming a high-protein diet. No clinical advice.
copy: An estimate based on blood creatinine is a different outcome from filtration measured with a separate tracer. An original creatine trial studied a particular group and used a direct clearance approach to examine filtration. That helps answer a narrower question about the study conditions.
Keep the marker and the estimate separate

If a paper reports only creatinine, check how it was interpreted and whether it also gave a filtration estimate or reference method. The numbers and units answer different questions. The tested group and measurement window also matter when comparing results.
An experimental result cannot interpret your individual lab reading. Use this distinction when checking whether a headline accurately describes what a published study measured.

article: Does more carnosine in muscle mean a cyclist finished faster?
Compare the tissue marker and the separate performance outcome in original beta-alanine research.
Original studies of beta-alanine, measured muscle carnosine and exercise endpoints. No regimen guidance.
copy: A beta-alanine study can measure carnosine in muscle and record exercise performance separately. An increase in the measured tissue compound is not itself a faster race time. Original studies measured carnosine alongside defined exercise tests to investigate both outcomes.
Find the event or exercise test in the methods

Check which test the researchers used. A fixed-power bout to exhaustion has a different endpoint from completing a set distance as quickly as possible. A marker change also does not specify whether the study detected a change in its exercise outcome.
Report the endpoint with the result. A finding in one test or group should not be retold as a time saving at every distance.
